question: Why does the Transformer scale dot-product attention by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$, and what are the exact dimensions $h$, $d_{\text{model}}$, $d_k$, $d_v$, and $d_{ff}$ in the base model?
expected: For large $d_k$, dot products grow large in magnitude (if components of $q$ and $k$ are independent random variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$, their dot product has mean $0$ and variance $d_k$), pushing the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients; scaling by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ counteracts this (Attention Is All You Need, Sec. 3.2.1, Footnote 1). The base model uses $h=8$ heads, $d_{\text{model}}=512$, $d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64$, and inner feed-forward dimension $d_{ff}=2048$ across $N=6$ encoder and decoder layers (Sec. 3.1, 3.2.2, 3.3, Table 3).

question: What optimizer parameters, warmup step count, dropout rate, and label smoothing value are used for the base Transformer, and how does label smoothing affect perplexity versus BLEU?
expected: The base Transformer uses Adam with $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.98$, $\epsilon=10^{-9}$, and $\text{warmup\_steps}=4000$ under learning rate schedule $d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5}\cdot\min(\text{step\_num}^{-0.5}, \text{step\_num}\cdot\text{warmup\_steps}^{-1.5})$ (Attention Is All You Need, Sec. 5.3, Eq. 3). It uses residual dropout $P_{\text{drop}}=0.1$ (whereas the big English-to-German model uses $0.3$ and big English-to-French uses $0.1$) and label smoothing $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$, which hurts perplexity because the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score (Sec. 5.4, Sec. 6.1, Table 3).

question: How does the Mimi neural audio codec convert a 24 kHz waveform into a 12.5 Hz latent representation at 1.1 kbps, and why does it use a split RVQ instead of a single 8-level RVQ?
expected: Mimi's SeaNet encoder cascades 4 causal convolutional blocks with striding factors $(4, 5, 6, 8)$ followed by a final 1D convolution with stride $2$ (total stride $1920$, or $80\text{ ms}$ per frame), projecting $24\text{ kHz}$ audio to $12.5\text{ frames/s}$ ($D=512$, projected to $256$ before RVQ) (Moshi, Sec. 3.3.1). With $Q=8$ quantizers of codebook size $N_A=2048$ ($\log_2(2048)=11\text{ bits}$), the bitrate is $12.5 \times 8 \times 11 = 1100\text{ bps} = 1.1\text{ kbps}$ (Sec. 3.3.1). Distilling WavLM semantic representations into the first level of a single RVQ degrades audio reconstruction because higher-order quantizers operate on the first quantizer's residual; Mimi solves this with a split RVQ combining 1 plain semantic VQ and a parallel 7-level acoustic RVQ whose outputs are summed, improving MUSHRA from $57.8$ to $64.0$ (Sec. 3.3.2, Table 3).
reply:
The Mimi codec first passes a 24 kHz raw waveform through a causal convolutional encoder that downsamples the signal by a factor of 2 in each of its four residual‑convolutional blocks with strides (4, 5, 6, 8) followed by a final 1‑D convolution with stride 2, yielding a latent sequence at 12.5 frames per second with a 512‑dimensional embedding for each frame [moshi-A-040].  Before vector quantisation, these embeddings are projected to 256 dimensions, the residual vector quantiser (RVQ) is applied, and the resulting code indices are projected back to 512 dimensions for the decoder [moshi-A-045].  Using eight RVQ codebooks each of size 2048 gives a bitrate of roughly 1.1 kbps at the 12.5 Hz sampling rate [moshi-A-045].

Mimi uses a split RVQ instead of a single 8‑level RVQ so that semantic information can be distilled into a plain VQ (the first codebook) while the remaining seven levels of a parallel RVQ encode acoustic details.  By summing the outputs of the two quantisers, Mimi removes the constraint that the residual of the semantic quantiser must preserve acoustic information, thereby improving the trade‑off between audio quality and phonetic discriminability [moshi-A-050].
citations: Moshi v1, §3.3.1 Architecture | Moshi v1, §3.3.2 Learning semantic-acoustic tokens with a split RVQ

question: In H-Net, how does the routing module compute boundary probabilities $p_t$ and discrete boundary indicators $b_t$, and what is the formula and weight $\alpha$ for the auxiliary ratio loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}$?
expected: The routing module projects encoder outputs $\hat{x}_t$ into queries $q_t = W_q\hat{x}_t$ and keys $k_t = W_k\hat{x}_t$, computing scaled cosine dissimilarity between adjacent positions: $p_t = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{\|q_t\|\|k_{t-1}\|}\right) \in [0,1]$, with $p_1 = 1.0$ by definition (the sequence begins with a boundary), and sets boundary indicator $b_t = \mathbf{1}_{\{p_t \ge 0.5\}}$ (Dynamic Chunking / H-Net, Sec. 2.2.1, Eq. 4). To guide compression toward target downsampling ratio $N$, H-Net adds the ratio loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}} = \frac{N}{N-1}\left((N-1)FG + (1-F)(1-G)\right)$, where $F = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^L b_t$ is the fraction of vectors selected and $G = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{t=1}^L p_t$ is the mean boundary probability; it is added to the autoregressive loss as $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{AR}} + \alpha\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}\mathcal{L}_{\text{ratio}}^s$ with $\alpha = 0.03$ fixed in all experiments (Sec. 2.2.3, Eq. 10).

question: Compare the tokenization approaches in all three papers, including vocabulary sizes, algorithms, and how each handles non-English languages or non-text modalities.
expected: 1) Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 5.1) uses static subword tokenizers: a shared source-target Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) vocabulary of ~37,000 tokens for WMT 2014 English-German (4.5M sentence pairs) and a 32,000 word-piece vocabulary for English-French (36M sentence pairs). 2) Moshi (Sec. 3.2.1, 3.3.1) uses a 32,000-token SentencePiece unigram text tokenizer (targeting English, splitting digits individually with byte-backoff) alongside Mimi, which tokenizes $24\text{ kHz}$ audio into 8 discrete codebooks of cardinality $2048$ at $12.5\text{ Hz}$. 3) H-Net (Sec. 1, 2.2, 3.2, Table 1, Table 4) eliminates handcrafted tokenizers entirely, operating directly on raw UTF-8 bytes (or A/C/G/T base pairs) and learning content-aware dynamic chunking end-to-end—achieving $4.7–4.8$ bytes/chunk (1-stage) and $6.9–7.0$ bytes/chunk (2-stage) on English, outperforming Llama-3 BPE on Chinese ($0.7032$ vs. $0.7404$ BPB; $66.3\%$ vs. $59.9\%$ XWinograd-zh) and code ($0.3161$ vs. $0.3376$ BPB), and reaching $3.6\times$ data efficiency on DNA.

question: Compare the optimizer choices, learning rate schedules, and parameter-group learning rate scaling across Attention Is All You Need, Moshi, and H-Net.
expected: 1) Attention Is All You Need (Sec. 5.3) uses Adam ($\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.98, \epsilon=10^{-9}$) with a 4,000-step linear warmup followed by inverse-square-root decay scaled globally by $d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5}$. 2) Moshi (Sec. 3.2.1, 3.3.1, 4.4, Table 1) uses AdamW across all stages: Helium pretrains with peak LR $3\cdot 10^{-4}$ and cosine decay; Mimi trains with LR $8\cdot 10^{-4}$ ($\beta_1=0.5, \beta_2=0.9$, EMA $0.99$) applying weight decay $5\cdot 10^{-2}$ *only* to Transformer parameters; and Moshi uses separate learning rates for the Temporal vs. Depth Transformers ($3\cdot 10^{-5}$ vs. $2\cdot 10^{-4}$ in pretraining; $3\cdot 10^{-6}$ vs. $5\cdot 10^{-5}$ in post-training; $2\cdot 10^{-6}$ vs. $4\cdot 10^{-6}$ on Fisher; $2\cdot 10^{-6}$ for both in instruct tuning) plus two separate optimizer states to balance text-only and audio batches. 3) H-Net (Sec. 2.3, Sec. 3, Appendix C, Eq. 11) uses AdamW with a Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedule ($10\%$ linear warmup, stable phase, $20\%$ inverse-square-root decay; base LR $6.25\times 10^{-4}$ for Large, $5.0\times 10^{-4}$ for XL) and modulates each hierarchical stage's LR by $\lambda^s = \sqrt{N^{\text{GPT}} \cdot \frac{\prod_{i=s}^S N^i}{\prod_{i=0}^S N^i} \cdot \frac{D^S}{D^s}}$ so outer stages processing longer sequences get higher learning rates.

question: In Moshi's safety evaluation, why does AudioSeal signal-based watermarking fail when tested against Mimi, why does token-level generative watermarking also fail, and how does Moshi eliminate verbatim training-data regurgitation?
expected: When AudioSeal-watermarked audio is compressed and decompressed through Mimi (or RVQGAN), the 10-second watermark detection score collapses from $0.9999$ to $0.0805$ ($0.2404$ on 1-minute audio), which is indistinguishable from unwatermarked audio ($0.0855$ / $0.2474$) because low-bitrate perceptual codecs discard non-reconstructive signal perturbations (Moshi, Sec. 6.4, Table 15). Generative token-sampling watermarks also fail because Mimi is not idempotent: re-encoding a generated waveform changes token indices (even at $\Delta T = 0$, only $76.6\%$ of semantic $k=1$ tokens and $26.4\%–55.0\%$ of acoustic $k=2..8$ tokens match, dropping to $48.3\%$ for $k=1$ under a $40\text{ ms}$ shift) (Sec. 6.4, Table 16). To prevent regurgitation of frequent training segments (which reaches $98.4\%–100\%$ on 3s-prompted raw single-stream models), Moshi deduplicates the training audio using mel-spectrogram constellation-map hashes ($2^{26}$ hash space with Hough 1D temporal voting, Appendix B), reducing the regurgitation rate to $0.00\%$ across $10^5$ generations (Sec. 6.2, Table 13, Appendix B).
